claims.text: The as-fabricated additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a homogeneous FCC matrix.
Elevated-temperature degradation is primarily governed by the stability and integrity of a protective surface oxide scale.
The protective scale is predominantly composed of Al2O3 and TiO2.
Under oxidizing conditions, formation of a continuous oxide scale initially slows degradation by limiting oxygen diffusion.
Cracking, discontinuity, or spallation of the oxide scale produces localized accelerated oxidation.
Grain boundaries are particularly vulnerable sites for oxide-scale discontinuity and oxygen ingress.
Oxygen ingress following scale failure drives internal and intergranular oxidation.
Internal and intergranular oxidation causes embrittlement and can lead to catastrophic failure.
Reducing atmospheres inhibit or destabilize formation of the passivating oxide scale.
The absence of a stable scale under reducing conditions enhances elemental diffusion along grain boundaries.
Elevated-temperature exposure can produce microstructural alteration or phase instability in compositionally related high-entropy alloys.
Under reducing conditions, microstructural instability and embrittlement will begin sooner than under oxidizing conditions.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure will initially decrease the degradation rate through protective-scale formation.
After oxide-scale integrity is compromised, oxidizing exposure will produce rapid degradation and catastrophic failure.
Before elevated-temperature exposure, the alloy has a naturally formed, continuous thin oxide film.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 600 degrees Celsius under sustained oxidizing or reducing atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures or in mixed or transitioning gas atmospheres.
